issues.legal_issue: A statutory restriction on revisional jurisdiction does not, by itself, bar the High Court from exercising supervisory jurisdiction over an order made by a subordinate appellate court.
material_facts: The High Court set aside a subordinate judge’s order granting an ad interim injunction on appeal.
The High Court acted under its supervisory jurisdiction, rather than under its writ or revisional jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The objection that the restriction on revisional jurisdiction deprived the High Court of authority to intervene was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The restriction in section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure concerns revisional jurisdiction where a right of appeal against the impugned order is available; it does not bar supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227. The Court also noted, relying on Aundal Ammal v. Sadasivan Pillai, (1987) 1 SCR 485, that a second revision does not lie against a subordinate court’s revisional order.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_supervisory_review: A party challenges the High Court’s review of a subordinate court order.
predicates.subordinate_order_was_appellate: The order reviewed by the High Court was made by a subordinate court exercising appellate authority.
predicates.high_court_used_supervisory_jurisdiction: The High Court acted in its supervisory capacity rather than exercising appellate or revisional authority.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns supervisory review of a subordinate appellate order, and the High Court acted in its supervisory capacity, the revisional restriction does not bar that review.

issues.legal_issue: An interim injunction cannot be used to protect a person with no legal right to remain in possession against the rightful owner.
material_facts: The property had been acquired, possession had been taken, and it had been handed to the public authority.
The occupants entered under leave-and-licence arrangements that had expired.
An eviction order against the occupants had become final, leaving them with no legal right to remain in possession.
The occupants relied on municipal resolutions that did not establish a prima facie right to retain the property.
The injunction would restrain the public authority from taking possession for the purpose for which the property had been acquired.
issues.conclusion: The occupants had no basis for an interim injunction against the rightful owner; there was neither a balance of convenience in their favour nor irreparable injury warranting relief. The High Court rightly dissolved the injunction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Shiv Kumar Chadha v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, (1993) 3 SCC 161, and Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh, (1992) 1 SCC 719, interim injunction is discretionary and requires a strong prima facie case, a favourable balance of convenience, and a risk of irreparable injury not adequately remedied by damages. A court must not use its process to protect or perpetuate a wrong, and an injunction cannot be granted against the rightful owner at the instance of persons in unlawful possession.

predicates.temporary_injunction_sought: A party seeks temporary injunctive relief while a suit is pending.
predicates.applicant_lacks_legal_right_to_possessio: The applicant has no legal entitlement to remain in possession of the property.
predicates.respondent_is_rightful_owner: The respondent is entitled to possession as the rightful owner.

issues.definition: When a party seeks a temporary injunction despite lacking a legal right to possession, and the respondent is the rightful owner, the injunction must be refused.

issues.legal_issue: When an injunction delays a public utility project and the plaintiff ultimately loses the suit, the trial court must assess the resulting damages, notwithstanding its ordinary pecuniary limits.
material_facts: The injunction delayed a project to widen a road for a public purpose for 24 years.
The delay caused the project’s costs to increase.
The Court directed that, if the suit was dismissed, the trial court assess the damages and enter a decree against the occupants.
issues.conclusion: If the suit is dismissed, the trial court must assess the damages caused by the injunction and decree recovery against the plaintiffs; its pecuniary jurisdiction is not an impediment to that assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Public interest is a material consideration in deciding whether to grant an interim injunction affecting public works. In exercising equitable jurisdiction, a court may compensate a defendant for loss caused by an injunction, and that consequential assessment is not barred by the court’s pecuniary jurisdiction. The Court relied on equitable and inherent jurisdiction principles and the cited legal commentary; it did not rely on an earlier case for this damages ruling.

predicates.interim_injunction_delayed_public_utilit: An interim injunction prevented or delayed work on a project serving a public utility.
predicates.plaintiff_later_loses_suit: The plaintiff ultimately fails to obtain the relief sought in the suit.

issues.definition: If an interim injunction delays a public utility project and the plaintiff later loses the suit, the trial court must assess the damages caused by the injunction.
